extracted.intended_audience: students, poets, and literary critics interested in poetics and the theory of poetry (Renaissance/Elizabethan)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes Renaissance-era evaluative principles about poetry: what poetry is, its kinds, its purposes, and how it differs from history and philosophy. Useful for judging or composing poetry according to Sidney/Aristotelian standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry is the one creative art
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with sciences/arts that 'repeat what they find' (e.g., astronomers). Emphasizes that poetry invents/creates rather than merely reporting or copying; poets generate new forms/ideas rather than simply restating observed facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poets improve Nature
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poets do not merely imitate nature but enhance or 'improve' it — idealizing features to present a heightened, exemplary form of human character or scene. This includes the related claim: "And idealize man." (footnote {14}) — the poet's role is to present an idealized humanity that instructs or moves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essence in thought, not in apparelling of verse
rubrics_metrics.description: "Its essence is in the thought, not in apparelling of verse." (footnote {22})
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should privilege the intellectual/substantive content (thought, imagination, general truth) over mere ornament, elaborate diction, or 'apparelling' (surface style). A poem's merit rests primarily on what it says and the ideas it embodies, not on verse-decoration alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry concerns what might be (general truth) vs. History's particular
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted Aristotle: "It is not by writing in verse or prose that the Historian and Poet are distinguished... The one relates what has been, the other what might be... Poetry is chiefly conversant about general truth; History about particular."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a criterion to judge a work: good poetry renders plausible, general truths (universal human behaviours, types, moral lessons) rather than merely chronicling specific factual events. The measure is the poem's treatment of universal plausibility and significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry advances virtuous action (moral purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Poetry best advances the end of all earthly learning, virtuous action." (footnote {26})
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One standard for evaluating poetry is its capacity to promote virtue and moral improvement. Sidney argues poetry has an advantage over Moral Philosophy and History in advancing virtuous conduct because of the poet's imaginative and exemplifying power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet's superiority to Philosopher and Historian (except the Divine)
rubrics_metrics.description: "In what manner the Poet goes beyond Philosopher, Historian, and all others (bating comparison with the Divine)." (footnote {31})
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: assess whether the poet's method (imagined exempla, representation of general truth) achieves understanding or moral persuasion that exceeds what philosophy or history can accomplish. The poet's imaginative capacity is a distinct evaluative virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of poetry: Divine, Philosophical, and Poetry proper
rubrics_metrics.description: Footnote listing: "§2. Its kinds. a. Divine. b. Philosophical, which is perhaps too imitative. c. Poetry proper." (footnote {17}-{20})
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use genre/type classification to judge aims and methods: divine poetry has religious/prophetic scope; philosophical verse risks being overly imitative of didactic philosophy; 'poetry proper' (dramatic/epic/lyric) differs in methods and ends. The note that 'philosophical is perhaps too imitative' flags a potential anti-pattern for evaluators: avoid poems that merely paraphrase philosophy without poetic transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subdivision and parts of the Poet's work (focus on 'what Poetry does for us')
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Poet’s Work and Parts. §1. WORK: What Poetry does for us." (footnote {24})
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate poetry by its functional parts and effects (how it instructs, moves, and molds behaviour). This rubric points evaluators to consider not just form but the poet's tasks/effects: illumination, moral instruction, memory, and pleasure combined to foster virtuous action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of hackneyed common-places
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of 'common-place' (footnote {34}): frequent resort to Polyanthea and common-places causes many good quotations to be hackneyed; 'a common-place' came to mean a trite saying, commonly without wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practical negative criterion: overuse of commonplace quotations or hackneyed sayings weakens poetic originality and wit. Original expression and avoidance of clichéd common-places are valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as 'first Light-giver' (enlightening function)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider poetry's enlightening function — its ability to illuminate truths and understanding. When evaluating or composing, give weight to the work's capacity to enlighten, to shed light on human nature or moral truths.
